utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please tell the Court your full name, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I am Rudy Gerritsen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are, I believe, a Lieutenant Colonel in the Royal Netherlands Army at present?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I propose to take you very briefly through some preliminary matters and we'll then get into the heart of your testimony which really begins at about paragraph 9 of the outline that we have prepared and which you signed yesterday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born on May 9, 1954 in the Netherlands, I believe?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are a Dutch citizen and you currently live in Almere with your wife and three teenage daughters.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a graduate of the Royal Netherlands Military Academy in 1976?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe two years ago you graduated from the University of Utrecht with a degree in business management.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you've been in the Royal Netherlands Army since the age of 18, since 1972?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your speciality in the military is as a logistics expert?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked at the information technology department at the Dutch Ministry of Defence during your 28-year military career?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Posting to Lebanon in 1981 during the civil war there, was followed in 1989 by a posting to Germany as a member of the Dutch army, and I believe you stayed there until 1992?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you have actually taught courses in your military speciality, logistics at Bussum in the Netherlands for two years between 1992 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of relevance today, I believe, you joined the European Community Monitoring Mission, the ECMM in June of 1993 and remained with that organisation until January of 1994 when you returned to your native country?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You work in Soesterberg as an account manager for special equipment in the Royal Netherlands Army?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, in your own words, prior to your assignment specifically to Bosnia-Herzegovina with the ECMM what training, what educational instruction, did you receive at the hands of either the Royal Netherlands Army or the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Prior to my assignment in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I received a week-long training session regarding the situation in Bosnia, former Yugoslavia. During that week, I was instructed in history, culture, economics and military situation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were also trained to use and deal with interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I might just interrupt a little bit, Lieutenant-Colonel, I think that you are referring to your statement, it would actually be helpful if you could do it in your own words.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we received three-week long training, and one week was training in The Hague where they talked about the political, economic, law and humanitarian matters and also military matters of former Yugoslavia, also the history of Yugoslavia and how we have to deal with the interpreters. It was, in my opinion, a training which was rather short, but helpful for us and I used a lot of material which we got on paper when I was that half year in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was quite helpful. The two-weeks military training, of course I am -- I was at that time almost 20 years in the army, so I was trained as a soldier, but not on the aspect of a civil war which was going on in Bosnia. In the two-weeks military training, we've got all kind of things, like recognition of mines, how we have to cope with roadblocks and such things, and just normal military stuff, medical aid and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What was the principal role that was being fulfilled by the ECMM in Bosnia-Herzegovina, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, the principal role of us as monitors was to be in the terrain, where we have to monitor political, military, and humanitarian matters. Political was a bit difficult for me, because I'm not a political guy, but we've got simple questions as what do the people think of the outcome of negotiations in the international forums. We ask that and then we get an answer and we report that to Zenica. Of course, we could see how the situation was in the field on military aspects and humanitarian aspects. We reported every day, a report to Zenica in Bosnia; Zenica reported to Zagreb; Zagreb reported to the -- how do you call that? -- the main cities in Europe, Canada, and so on, on the memos of that community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a monitor in the field, so to speak, Lieutenant Colonel, did you or your colleagues have any role in attempting to mediate disputes between the warring factions themselves?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did, all kind of matters, like a change of the bodies, POWs, humanitarian aspects, if they wanted to have medicines, all these kind of things that were -- they had a lack of. And a lot of things were -- was negotiating. For example, if we wanted to visit a prison camp of POWs or civilians, mostly we didn't get in. But if we had an exchange, for example, POWs or bodies from the other party, we could get in. So it was a lot of negotiation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe that you also became involved with humanitarian aid matters on both sides, the --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, on both sides. We also talked with UNHCR, ICOC, and other agencies who were at the time in Bosnia. Because in my area of responsibility, which was Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and the war was going on after mid-July in Bosnia, in that area of responsibility, it was hard to get in for humanitarian agencies, so we spoke to them and we got some materiel and brought them in in the more dangerous areas. We did that together with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get into specific incidents and crimes later in your testimony in a fairly brief way, but just generally, Lieutenant Colonel, did the ECMM have any role actually in the investigation of crimes for purposes of future war crimes investigations, or not?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, not specifically. Of course, we reported the things we saw, but it wasn't the aim at that moment to make specific investigations of war crimes. I was more -- I dealt more with humanitarian matters. But if we saw some, we reported them, but we were not trained to investigate such specific matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've previously described and the Court's heard a lot of evidence about how the monitoring teams were organised in the reporting chain up through the regional centres, and you've previously described that the regional centre to which you reported was located in Zenica. And I believe that while you were present in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were two heads of that regional centre, the first being Jean-Pierre Thebault and the second being Sir Martin Garrod.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you understood it, was Ambassador Thebault a soldier? Did he have a military background?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Ambassador Thebault, Pierre Thebault, was not a military guy. He was a nice man, fine man, I think. I met him not often. When I came in, I met Thebault; when I went out from the area of Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, Prozor; and once in between. So I met him totally, I think, three times, and I spoke to him and he was a nice guy, I think. But he was not a military man and we didn't see him in the field, contrary to Mr. Garrod, Sir Garrod. He was a military man who was a monitor before he became head of Zenica, and I could speak more easily with him about certain matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just move on to the next subject, the reports that you prepared. Could you just describe for the Trial Chamber the process by which you prepared reports, to whom they were submitted, and what happened to those reports, in your experience in the country after they had been submitted to your superiors.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We made every day daily report. And it was sent by CapSat to RC Zenica. There they put together all the reports from several teams. And so it was a compilation of several reports, a shortage. And after that it went to Zagreb and there they made report of the several RCs, which also was a shortage, and that was sent to the capital cities. And my opinion of what I saw was that very often only one line or no lines of our reports were in the report which finally came back from Zagreb. So we did our job, and sometimes nothing was said about our job. And that was sometimes disappointing, but it is not always interesting to report to the capital cities what we have seen, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, I believe that you kept on your own computer an electronic version of all of the reports that you prepared, and you have provided the Kordic Defence, me and my colleagues, with access to these reports; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would have, I take it, no difficulty in providing the Prosecution with access to the same reports?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Say again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would have no difficulty in allowing the Prosecution, the people on the other side --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, no. Not at all. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a matter of interest. Have you ever been contacted by the investigators or by the Prosecution in this or in any other case to --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're very grateful for the fact that you've provided these reports, Mr. Gerritsen, because we've been trying for two years to persuade the ECMM to give us documents, so far without success.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I may -- Your Honour, we have prepared two packages of exhibits, the first consisting of military informations summaries prepared by the Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire, which we'll refer to very briefly in this case in the examination, and the second consists of a selected package of Mr. Gerritsen's reports, which will allow the Trial Chamber to go chronologically quickly through his testimony. If I could just have these numbered, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The bundle with the ECMM reports will be marked D284/1, and the bundle of milinfosums will be marked D285/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, in the package of documents marked D284/1 this is a compilation of your reports, I'd just like to draw your attention to two entries in Tabs 1 and 2 which describe the situation in Bugojno, one of the three main municipalities in your area of responsibility before the fighting broke out there in mid-July of 1993. Just turning your attention to Tab 1 of your exhibits here under paragraph 2, it says, "Relations between the Croats and Muslims in Bugojno continue to appear very good." This is as of July 2, 1993, could you just elaborate upon that to the Trial Chamber. What was the political and military situation amongst the Croats and the Muslims in the town of Bugojno as far as you saw it in the very early part of your tour of duty in the area, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that I came in the -- I believe the 16th of July and then the clashes started, so what I saw is what I heard. The situation between the Croats and Muslims there was quite stable. They were negotiating about civil matters and there were no problems at that point there. A year before, they fought against the Bosnian Serbs, the front line with the Bosnian Serbs. The outcome of the front line of the Bosnian Serbs was in the neighbourhood of Bugojno and the Croats and Muslims fought together against the Bosnian Serbs and -- so that was the situation there at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- you're telling us that you arrived on July 16th which, I believe, was just two or three days before the heavy fighting, actually.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: One day before the clashes started. I arrived on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just take a look at the second tab --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: And I came there, maybe it's interesting to say, because they got in Zenica because first I should go to Tuzla and then they -- the military people and intelligence from RC Zenica has heard that there were reinforcements in the surroundings of Bugojno, probably they had seen Mujahedin and several brigades so it could be interesting, and monitor team in Gornji Vakuf should be reinforced and then they sent me in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But what you are telling us, I think, is that you had been briefed and you had heard from your colleagues that the political and military situation insofar as Croat and Muslim cooperation in Bugojno was concerned was amicable and without evident problems, imminent hostilities?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, they expected no war at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just take a look at the second tab of Exhibit D284/1, sir, this is another daily report I think that was generated one day before you arrived. Paragraph 2 describes a political meeting held in Bugojno and the upshot of the meeting was that the local politicians decided that they would continue with two parallel authority structures until there is a new political solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that your understanding of the way in which the municipality was being run with two separate power structures, if you like, one Croat and one Muslim within one municipality?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, it was that way at that time. Later on, I think one or two months later, they started again with this structure, with these structures, so it --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next tab, Tab 3, is a report that was generated on the day that you arrived. And in the first paragraph, there is a reference to what you've just referred to, Mujahedin soldiers in Bugojno and soldiers from the 7th Muslim Brigade on the border between the municipality of Bugojno and Travnik municipality. This basically reflects what you saw yourself with your own eyes when you arrived in the area, does it?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see any Mujahedin. When I came in, I didn't see the 7th Muslim Brigade, it's only of hearing because I came in that day, and I was only held up in Novi Travnik where I was shot by Muslim snipers at a T-junction in Novi Travnik so I had a delay that day, and I came in on Sunday afternoon. And that was the situation and that they were seeing Mujahedin was already known at RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And your colleagues who drafted this particular report presumably told you about the sightings of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Skat Rordan he was Danish guy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were claims being made as you can see at the bottom of the page by the HVO in Bugojno that there was incidents of rape and plunder taking place in the Croat villages and municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you turn to the next exhibit, sir, July 19th, 1993, very briefly in paragraph 3 and paragraph 8, there are only two points I would like to draw to your attention. The first is that there is a contemporaneous record obviously of the -- that fighting had started. Was this light skirmishing or was this full-scale warfare?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It was full-scale warfare at that moment in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the observation is made by you and your colleague, Mr. Skat Rordan?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It was only made by me because Skat Rordan, had a problems with a Warrior from the British that we were arriving with, and so particularly at that date, happened that I went alone with the UNPROFOR to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that no clear picture of the fighting in Bugojno had emerged to you?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is a -- this is paragraph 10 of the outline, Your Honours, you make the observation that you do not know the exact cause of the ABiH offensive but you give your views on the military fighting that occurred in that area, and I wonder if you could just give your views to the Trial Chamber, in your own words, about your perceptions of the causes of the fighting and its progress in the immediate days?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, when I came in the first day, the fighting was going on on a large scale. We saw several soldiers acting like soldiers, shooting and hiding and covering, and that was the not clear picture because we couldn't see which direction they were going at that time, at that particular day. The next days, we saw that the BiH had an out number of people and they were conquering first Bugojno, the town itself. And they were quite successful with the help at that time of Senad Dautovic, which was a policeman, and other situation in Bugojno very well, and they managed to isolate the Croats in Bugojno. In the surroundings of Bugojno, in the fields, we couldn't get in, so we could only see what we saw from the main road from Gornji Vakuf to Bugojno, and each day, they came more in the direction of Gornji Vakuf. So the conclusion you can make as military men is that they were gaining ground and the Croats were in a bad -- were in bad circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you there, just so that we can give the Trial Chamber an identification of the actual local military units, I believe, the local military unit on the ABiH side in Bugojno was the 307th Brigade under the command of Tahir Granica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness give the evidence.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The specific units I have to look up in the files because I never get them in my head which specific brigade is where on the terrain. There are all kinds of maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me see if I can help you. Can you turn to Exhibit D285/1 which is the compilation of the milinfosums prepared by BritBat Tab 2, page 2, paragraph 8 there actually identifies the commanders and the brigades.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, this one which I met later on, what I can say more and -- on a more abstract level is that the BiH had more soldiers. They had, I think, about six or seven brigades and the Croats up there had only two brigades. So the Croats were outnumbered by the BiH and each unit has a number and at that time, we have made specific organisations, military stuff, and that information we've got and you could see the results in the fields of that because they were gaining ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: To gain ground, you have to have three times more people and materiel than the defending party because otherwise it's very difficult to gain any ground and we could see that in the organisations which we had on paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that force ratio, did that kind of force ratio exist in the Bugojno area in favour of the attacking ABiH troops?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, that force ratio existed, yes; seven, two, two, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just two questions in connection with the British milinfosum here, did you meet Tahir Granica, the commander here?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The commander of the 307 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I met him later when he was captured as POW.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever meet Ivica Lucic?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, no, I met -- let me see, I met Ivica Lucic, sorry, a field commander of the Edvard Kvaternik Brigade; he was captured. And I didn't meet Tahir Granica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to your conversations with local Croats, was any information imparted to you as to whether they had been prepared for conflict or fighting with the Muslim adversaries or not? If that question is unclear, I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, I read the question. Sometimes I need some time because I don't speak English every day, you know. They have been prepared for conflict of fighting with the Muslim -- it isn't clear for me what you are meaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We know that the HVO and the Muslims had been combining together to fight the Bosnian Serb army on the front lines with that institution, but did you receive any information from Croats whether they had been preparing for a fight with Muslims at around this time of 1993 or not?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't receive any information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You make the observation in your outline here that the Muslim forces conquered the HVO-held positions in several days and you testified to that today. If we could just go very briefly through some of the reports that you prepared contemporaneously. Turning to Tab 5 of the ECMM documents, paragraph 3, there's the observation that Bugojno was nearly at the stage where it is not even safe to go in in Warriors, that the BiH --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit exaggerated, I think. It's never safe -- it's never safe to go into war, of course, and but the Warrior was quite safe. You always take risks at that moment, and -- well, that's our job mainly. And sometimes it was quite -- it is an understatement -- interesting to be there as a military officer. What's safe? I think it's a bit exaggerated, because we have by ourselves always the impression that they didn't aim specifically at us. That was our feeling at that time. So we felt quite safe. But it wasn't safe to go with our own vehicles from the ECMM at that time. The war is well shot with small arms and not with anti-tank grenades or something like that. So it is always difficult to say, is it safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Court already knows that a Warrior is an armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It is an armoured vehicle from the British army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the assessment that was made by the BiH people to whom you spoke, or the ABiH soldiers, around the 21st of July, was that they would have control over the town within the next two days, within the next 48 hours?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. But also they get a delay. It was some days later, but -- before they succeeded. It was just an assessment at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And if you turn to tab 6, under to the military activity section, you say that every possible weapon except atomic bombs are being used in the battle, but that steadily and easily the ABiH was gaining control over the town. Was that your observation as to the course of the heavy fighting, with the exception of the nuclear analogy?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was a real war going on. For me, as a monitor -- it may be specific as a Dutch monitor. I do not know, of course. But it was quite disturbing that I was suddenly -- I came in from Holland and I was in the war and it was a real war. So on one hand it was interesting for a military person; on the other hand, it's a war, and sometimes you are frightened. And all possible weapons I know of were used. But it's of course a bit humour in a daily report to RC Zenica, but to stress the feeling of our meaning, of our opinion, that real war was going on and they were fighting tough up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to touch very lightly and briefly on the next two exhibits in the ECMM document package that we've put together, tab 7 is a report dated July 25th, 1993. And under paragraph 3, the observation is made that it is believed that the HVO are just about finished in Bugojno. And then two days later, tab 8, you make the observation, with your colleague, Mr. Hauenstein --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Hauenstein. Canadian guy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that in Bugojno it is a different story. The BiH control the complete town. And then later in paragraph 3 you make the observation that militarily the ABiH goal was to finish off the HVO in the area.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that happen?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: As far as Bugojno, yes. Not in all our area of responsibility, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to turn to the question of prisoners of war, paragraph 13 of your outline makes the observation that several hundred HVO soldiers became prisoners of war, and you also describe a conversation with a commander, or former commander at this time, of the 1st Battalion of the Edvard Kvaternik Brigade. Could you just tell the Trial Chamber what you remember about that conversation specifically and the plight of prisoners of war, that you saw, generally?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, when we came in at that particular spot with our Warrior, we went out and -- before I'm going on, is that the first time I spoke when -- at the moment he was taking as -- he was taken prisoner as POW?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just describe the conversation --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Okay. At that moment. Yes. We left the Warrior to make some -- to see what was going on, and at that time there was a lot of shootings. It was quite dangerous. We walked around, and because of the shooting we went under cover and we took another road, just a couple of metres, of course. Maybe you can imagine that situation. And because we didn't take the normal road, we saw suddenly 40 POWs on the ground --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't need the details. If you could just describe the conversations that you had with this man, that would be helpful. We don't have unlimited time.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It's interesting for me. Just memories, you know. Sorry. And then we went to the POWs what was going on there, and our question to the POWs was: "Are you treated well as POW?" That was the question we had at that time. And the other people told me that that man was the battalion commander, so we spoke to him and spoke to the battalion commander, and he said that at that time he was just taken POW and there were beatings and -- but not very severe. It was a short conversation. And what he told me at that time was he asked me if I could visit him in prison, I remember, and that day -- and some talk about why they surrendered to the Muslims, to the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That was mainly the conversation. It was quite disturbing. Of course, at that time he was frightened and -- a lot of soldiers, yes. It's not a conversation on a high level or something like that, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever have occasion to see this man subsequently?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him about 14 days later when I visited POW camp, and what -- and that POW, it was in the basement of a school. The circumstances were bad. And suddenly at the time I saw the same man. And we saw each other and we spoke -- we have spoken to each other in the basement of that school. I saw he was beaten up. He had bruises up here and bandages around, I believe, his arm or something. And he had these bruises and bandages at the time I saw him, when he was taken POW, two weeks before. So it was at that time clear for us that they were treated not well as POW, like they should regarding the Geneva Conventions. So that was our observation and we reported that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to visit another detention facility at the soccer stadium in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I was there twice in the soccer stadium, and the same bad circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If we could touch very lightly on this, Lieutenant Colonel. There are two reports that you've prepared that we've included in the package. Tab 11, paragraph 4, you make some reference to, under the humanitarian activity section, to the fact that the ABiH have now admitted that they had four POW cages in Bugojno, about three or four hundred people incarcerated there, the ABiH admitting that some of the POWs had been beaten and contending that one such POW had been killed while trying to escape. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: They always tried to escape and then got killed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next tab, tab 12, under the humanitarian activities section there, you make a reference to visiting five Croat POWs in a hospital in Bugojno --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- who had been beaten on their backs. You saw great spots of effusions of blood, and the POWs told you that the prisoner who had died, reported in the report we just looked at, actually died as a result of a beating and not in the endeavour of trying to escape.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. That was interesting because of the different declarations by the BiH and by these five POWs, Croat POWs, so we reported this, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you make a reference to detention conditions and your conclusions regarding them in paragraph 15 of the outline that you signed yesterday. I don't propose to go over that with you. Everyone can read that. And if the Prosecution has any questions about that, then they can certainly ask you about that. What I'd like to turn to now is the condition in which the Croat civilians found themselves. According to the 1991 census, Bugojno had a total population, I believe, of 46.889, 16.000 of whom were Croats. How many of these Croats actually fled from the municipality in the face of the ABiH military attack in mid-July of 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: About 12.000 or more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what happened to the three or four thousand or so that remained in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We had a lot of negotiation about that. They were treated not well all the time, and it was quite confusing for us, because the Muslims and the BiH always said that the Croats were welcome in Bugojno, although 12.000 had fled, and it was not their intention to have ethnic cleansing and the Croats were still welcome in their city, Bugojno. But from the Croats, the minority in Bugojno, we heard the several -- how do you call it? -- allegations they had: There was raping, they were brutalised, they were kicked out of their houses. So it was a hard time at that time for the Croat minority in Bugojno. Well, that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many civilians were killed during this offensive, as far as you understand, approximately, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I'm very bad at numbers, but I think 40, something like that. It's in the file somewhere, but I think 40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's just go through --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: And 170 soldiers, I think. Oh, here, it is, yes. One hundred and seventy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to tab 9 of your package of exhibits here, page 2. The note is made that V2 observed the looting and burning of houses by BiH soldiers in the town of Humac. I take it that -- who was V2?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: V2, that was our team. V2 was called Victor 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you observed incidents like this yourself?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And if you turn to the next exhibit, or tab, the next tab, tab 10 --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Tab 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a -- under the humanitarian activity section there's an observation that the Croats in Bugojno are worried for the future. They lack supplies. They claim that they are being robbed from on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that consistent with the sorts of conditions that you were hearing?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That was consistent, because we spoke at that time a lot of people, and such messages are confirmed several times, and we could see the results of beatings and robbings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just a few more --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We were there on a daily basis, and so you get a clue of the circumstances in the town, in the field, and you see differences every day. And so you get I think a clear picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you could turn to tab 13, sir. It's a report dated August 12th of 1993 that you and your colleague prepared. On the first page the claim is made or the -- you report that the BiH policy in Bugojno states that: "They want Croats to live with them in peace, despite the fact that 12.000 had left. However, at the lower levels, this has been very difficult to implement. Further incidents have been brought forward of beatings, rapes, robberies, and killings."

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the one hand, you had the public declarations of the ABiH officials. How effective were the Muslim officials now in control of Bugojno in actually implementing this policy that was articulated to you of wanting Croats actually to live with them in peace and harmony in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: They were not successful, of course, at that time. It was too tense short after the fightings. There was a lot of hate, and these things are not successful, although I would not say that there couldn't be an attention to reach such goals on a long term. The political influences, it's hard to have a certain appreciation of the political influences up there and if they are correct. My opinion is that because 12.000 Croats were expelled, the political aim was to say, "Oh, you are welcome, of course. No problem. Come in." Because the political aim was to -- that was our feeling at that time -- to show the world that they had good meanings for the future on a long term. And what we saw on the ground was something different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Along those lines, Lieutenant Colonel, could I just ask you to turn to tab 14. Under the political situation column of your August the 15th, 1993 report, you make the observation that the presidency of Bugojno have now stated that it is official policy that Croats cannot leave Bugojno of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us the context of the declaration that have official policy?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I think the policy from above was to show that in Bosnia, the three populations, Muslims, Croats, Serbs could live together, that was the intention of the political intention of Izetbegovic at that time. He told the world as that. So they had to show that they cooperate and Bugojno there were almost no Serbs, only Croats and Muslims almost, that they could live together and work together. So the circumstances for the Croat minority the 2.000 or 3.000 who live there were bad, and they wanted to flee at that time. And it was political not correct good to show at that moment to the world that there were no Croats at all left in Bugojno. So I think that's the deeper meaning of this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you turn to the next page of this Tab, sir, you make the assessment that the Muslims in Bugojno will start applying more pressure to the remaining Croat community as information is received on the status of other Muslims in the country. And that was your view at that time, I take it?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And if you just turn to the next exhibit, there's a report that you prepared some days later on the 20th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no need to take too much time with this and just for the Trial Chamber's reference I'd also like to draw to your attention, Your Honours, on the milinfosum compilation Tab 8, page 1, the same sorts of reports are made by the British soldiers in the region. But this particular report, sir, details the allegations of murders, rapes, beatings, and so forth. That speaks for itself. But the -- you contemporaneously reported on this, did you?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you are aware, was anyone ever held accountable or responsible for any of these murders, rapes, beatings, things of that variety?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, there was no trials going on at that time like here. But we spoke to the police officer there, it's also on the same report, Senad Dautovic and, of course, we got some declarations for him and investigations ongoing. And sometimes they even said okay, we have done that and we will punish the people who have done these crimes, but we never saw any results.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did you ever hear that the few remaining Croats living in the municipality, that they had ever been told that these investigations were ongoing?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that measures were being taken?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, the Croats by themselves, in this case, specifically Father Janko, who was the priest in Bugojno, he talked with Dautovic and he handed this kind of material over to Senad Dautovic and we talked and so -- and so we were talking all together about the same stuff and they were allowed to speak. I also think to give them a feeling of safteyness [sic] at that time because the war was over at a certain amount.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to the next exhibit, Tab 16, I'm not saying exhibit, it's the next tab under the humanitarian activity section, second paragraph on page 1, it says, "The BiH Bugojno have reemphasized their requirements for the region; food, water and fuel." The BiH representative stated that if there are no sufficient basic needs, food, et cetera, Muslim people will start to rob Croat families. And the comment is made that this is probably one of the reasons to keep a Croat minority in Bugojno. Now, was that your view at that time that this report was written?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, it's a reason too, but we were never sure, of course, they won't tell us some things, but it's possible reason, sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in the next tab, sir, just to round off this line of questioning, Tab 17, under the political situation section, you make the observation that although the civil and military authorities in Bugojno had expressed a desire to reintegrate the Croat minority into the mainstream, there had been a general increase in violence against this group with a number of beatings and one murder. And that's an accurate recitation of what you were seeing on that day?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally on this line, September 13th, 1993, Tab 18, a meeting, I believe held in Bugojno, where the political party of the Croats, the HDZ expressed its main aim as that of saving Croat lives in the community and they wished, therefore, to maintain a good relationship with the city's civil war Presidency. And then, I believe, a conversation that occurred in Prozor, the civil and military authorities in Prozor did not support the reintegration of the Croat minority into Bugojno because they were asking whether these people would live, all of the houses had been burned.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: What was the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that an accurate recitation of the views that were being articulated to you by the political and military leaders in Bugojno and Prozor around this time?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. They told us so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: You asked not my meaning about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, you should let the witness -- you should give the witness the opportunity to tell us about these events in his own words rather than to tell it in his name, to say it in his name and then ask him to confirm it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very much so, Your Honour, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give the Trial Chamber, sir, in a -- in just a few words your views on the situation that you saw during these months following the offensive; the civil and military authorities on the one hand saying we would like to see all of the Croats stay or come back and then the actual realities of the situation with murders, rapes, house burnings, lootings, things of that variety. What kind of tension did you see in those two phenomena, what was being said and what was being done?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, there was a kind of a willingness from the Muslims to have the Croats in Bugojno, maybe because of political reasons I told already. I think it's correct to say that people on a certain level can always influence on the ground. We have criminals in Holland, in our country too, but my opinion was that in that country, former Yugoslavia, in a time of war, they have a specific way to the warfare, and that one of them is intimidation. And when you are raping and looting, you are getting people out of town on a -- well, that's one reason. To let people do what you want them to do, you can use these kind of what we call war crimes or some crimes. It's helpful for your aims at that time. Not all houses in Bugojno from the Croats were burned, but a lot of houses were burned, not all houses. So what they say in Prozor -- but I can understand the feeling from the Croats in Prozor. I also can understand the feelings of Muslims in Bugojno when they are talking about Muslims in Prozor and so on. That is the situation, atrocities on both sides, and that's the way they are doing their warfare. And I think specifically in Bugojno, the Croats were a minority and they were very frightened because they have notice of what warfare in their country is, so they were scared, of course, and they wanted to flee. Although maybe for political reasons, the Muslims, at that time, wanted a Croat minority to reintegrate in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Izetbegovic told very often so on television at that time. It was an aim. And all these things, then you have also hate because of the war, and as for the people living in that town, Bugojno, also very disturbing, I think. It was for us, as monitors, disturbing, but also for the people who are living there. And it was not clear for us how directly they are directed by higher levels. So sometimes we reported in this situation what the several people in several towns said that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir, if I can just try to speed up a little bit here, I'm going to pass over paragraph 17 and 18 of your outline and touch upon very briefly, the part of your outline that deals with Muslim versus Croat forces. Could you just give the Trial Chamber a feel for the degree of organisation you saw comparing the HVO to the ABiH. Which one was better organised in your view?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It was obviously the time that the Muslims specifically in the surroundings of Bugojno, as far as I could see, were better organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: And also their discipline was better, that their uniforms looked better, you know. As a military man, I say, okay, that's quite an army at that time, but contrary, the Croats were less sophisticated, rough, and they were louder when they spoke and -- that was the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that lack of sophistication flow over into relations, for example, with the International Community or the international media?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. As we always said, the Muslims played their cards better at that time, much better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of media control or what, could you give us some examples?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, media controls and also in the conversations with us. They, you know, when we spoke to the Croats, sometimes not the minority in Bugojno, but somewhere else, in Prozor or something like Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, there was more struggle. They became anger [sic] from time to time. They wanted us something to do and we were not allowed to bring packages or something like that and then they became anger and that was not a way the Muslims were acting. So a lot of people, I think, at that time, had a feeling that -- had that feeling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, to turn to a specific example, Gornji Vakuf, for example, do you have any observations regarding the way that the Croat side or the Muslim side used the civilian population for military advantage that you can help us with?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Our opinion was that the Muslims held the civilian people in Gornji Vakuf in Gornji Vakuf because of the shelling, and civilians get wounded or get killed, and it was good for the news outcome in the world because they were suffering. That's one -- that's what they wanted to let see the world, that was our opinion, because we have reasons to believe that it was possible for the civilian -- the Muslim civilians living in Gornji Vakuf to go out of Gornji Vakuf but they were not allowed, and that's strange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the Croat civilian population in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: They left and went to other places. So the outcome was that only military people were left from the Croats in Gornji Vakuf and only a few civilians, medical aid and such kind of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You make some observations regarding reliability of intelligence reports received from the Croat side and the Muslim side in paragraph 21, but I don't propose to go into that. In terms of the military leadership of the Muslim forces as opposed to the HVO forces, do you have any observations regarding the level of experience, military experience one side versus the other that you can help us with?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Military leadership of the Muslims was better at that time. We could speak more easily with the military Muslim commanders -- Selmo, I don't remember his last name. He has --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cikotic, would that help jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I think you are correct. But it was always nice to speak with him, you know, and it was difficult to speak with the military commanders of the HVO. You could not always rely on appointments you made. You also could not rely on appointments you made with the Muslim side but they apologised. Most of the times they were there. That was the difference. And on the HVO side, I spoke fairly often with Colonel Siljak and Praljak two times, two or three times, and -- he was harsh big man, you know, but I could speak to him because I was speaking some German language. And he liked to speak German language, he was very -- a man of theatre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to paragraph 25 of your outline and turn your attention to September 15th, 1993. Did you have occasion, yourself, to travel to the village of Uzdol and prepare a report that is attached as Tab 19 to Exhibit D284/1?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Uzdol on the 15th and it happened on the 14th and we were invited by the mayor of Prozor together with the UNPROFOR, BBC and other agencies, I think Reuters, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were interviewed by a BBC reporter.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the Court's permission we have a short video which I'd like marked as the next exhibit which shows the circumstances at Uzdol, and it is a TV interview that Lieutenant Colonel Gerritsen gave?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It's only a small part of it because my wife in Holland had no chance -- oh, that's me -- to get the whole interview to get the whole interview on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I could ask the technical booth to show the videotape that's been provided, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, if I can just finish up very briefly, the three final portions of your outline, did you or your colleagues in the ECMM in Bosnia-Herzegovina ever have, to your knowledge, any definitive proof of the presence of Croatian army units, soldiers in the territory of the country?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, we spoke a lot about it. It was always the discussion and it appeared to be for us fairly logical that there would be HV involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we never have seen at that time such influences nor materiel or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you put the question as to whether there was definitive proof and he answered no. Could he elaborate on that definitive proof would seem to suggest that there might have been some evidence but not reaching that level. Could he say what evidence there was, if any at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First there was a -- I have never seen any evidence of that kind in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we didn't find it fairly logical but we didn't find anything. We asked several people, we asked, for example, General Praljak about that, and it was always denied and we didn't saw anything. And we couldn't imagine that there was no involvement, but we didn't find anything. But I also have to say that my area of responsibility was relatively small. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two final points, Lieutenant Colonel, the contention has been made in this case that the Croats through their political institutions and military organisations engaged in a widespread and systematic policy or campaign of persecution of Bosnian Muslims in the country. You were present in the Bugojno, Prozor, Tomislavgrad, Gornji Vakuf area yourself for quite a while, for nearly six months or perhaps a little longer than that. Did you ever see any evidence of such a policy being implemented by Bosnian Croats against Muslims, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Policy, what's policy? This certain point. I saw a lot of things, and I also saw expelling of Muslims out of houses in my area of responsibility in Prozor. So -- but not at that amount of the expelling of people in Bugojno and when a war is going on and you see always that there is a lot of hate and when one people is doing one thing to another, and other people is doing something back, it's not like we should -- we -- supposed to act but people do. So I also saw expelling of Muslims by Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the town of Bugojno specifically, who was persecuting whom, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Muslims were persecuting Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout your stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you ever hear the name of Dario Kordic mentioned at all?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in Bugojno at any time?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you are aware, did anyone, any of the interlocutors with whom you were speaking, any of the soldiers, politicians anyone indicate that he had any kind of influence in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, they never talked about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Lieutenant Colonel. Thank you Your Honours, no further questions. Could we have a number for the videotape?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The videotape will be marked D286/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no questions for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, we're going to adjourn now for half an hour. Could you remember, please, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over and don't let anybody speak to you about it. If you will be back, please, at half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the tone of the summary served last night led us to prepare two bundles of documents, but the nature of the evidence given today means that we'll only have to look at a limited number of them, I'm happy to say, and I should hope to be completed really quite quickly with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I understand there's a matter you want to raise with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it's convenient, I'd like a short period of time after evidence on a couple of administrative matters inter parte; and thereafter, yes, if it's convenient, a very short hearing ex parte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be convenient. It would be even more convenient if we could do it before the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll do what I can. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, just a few questions before we look at some more documents. And one: You saw no Mujahedin yourself, but is it right that Croats speaking of ABiH and Muslims used the word "Mujahedin"?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if and when that appears in any of the reports that we are going to look at, can you explain how the word came to be used? It wouldn't have been ECMM policy to use the word "Mujahedin," so it must have come from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, I think the word "Mujahedin" is more sporadic than only in the context of ECMM. It's a word I knew before I entered ECMM. And I can only say that it was used. And I didn't see Mujahedin in my area of responsibility; I saw Mujahedin when I travelled from my area of responsibility to RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Right. That's fine. Second question: You spoke of the Muslims' better ability at dealing with public relations and so on. I'm not in a position to challenge what you say about that, but of course if they had better abilities in your area dealing with public relations, you made allowances for that when you wrote your reports; you weren't persuaded by them just simply because they were better at presenting themselves to you?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, no, I wasn't persuaded by that; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made the point -- and I just want to be sure I understand it -- towards the end of the period of time that you're referring to, it was quite clear to you that at the Izetbegovic level, for sure, there was a policy of multiethnicity.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Your Honour, what we've done is we've prepared two bundles, one which relates to events apparently within the Colonel's period of experience there, or just before, July 1993. Although these documents weren't prepared by him, I'd like his comment on some of them. And then we have another bundle of documents that he prepared himself. Because of the time restraints on us, they haven't been page numbered, but I think we can work our way through them without too much difficulty. So if we can look at the first set first, it's 2827. And Colonel, what I'm trying to do is just to look at contemporaneous documents for purposes other than those that were explored by Mr. Sayers this morning and to try and put things in some context, but we certainly shan't be looking at all the documents that we have before us. Your Honour, I don't know if it would be appropriate for the usher to be by the ELMO and to try to follow matters. Have we got another set for him, for the usher?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if he could place the documents on the ELMO from time to time. And if the witness can at least follow with his own copy, it will save time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what we're looking at simply on the first page of this, so that we can get context, is the 7th of July. And at that time, as we see under the general situation, Bugojno was slightly tense, sporadic shelling from the BSA. And that's your understanding of the history of the matter?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go on three pages, we find ourselves on the second sheet of a report for the 8th of July. Yes, 8th of July at the top. This is a report -- and we go to paragraph 9 on the second sheet. Thank you -- where your former monitor said that he visited the HVO in Prozor to establish facts about Muslim males held in custody. Do you have a recollection that Muslim males were being held in custody in Prozor at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And later on also, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the next page brings us to the 9th of July, and what we see in the developing story, under 1, the general situation, is that Bugojno was slightly tense, with inhabitants saying, "As well as the sun will rise in the morning, the Serbs will shell us today." But then further down, under 3, military activity, the HVO commander in Gornji Vakuf was saying that full-scale war was inevitable in Gornji Vakuf and likely to start in four days' time, and that the Armija commanders had high morale. Does that fit with your understanding of the history at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then if we go over two pages, we come to the 11th of July, just to see the developing picture in your part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And under military activity for the 11th of July, approximately 40 young, 18- to 20-year-old HVO soldiers observed doing training, with identical weapons and uniforms for the most part. This was all part of the build-up. Two pages further on, to the 12th of July, we see a record of a break in the shelling, under paragraph 1, at the fourth line: "Bugojno hasn't been shelled since the 9th of July." But what we -- yes. I needn't trouble with the other reference. So a gap in the shelling. And over two pages, to the 13th of July, this, under the general situation: "Prozor is calm, but active as normal." I'm trying to listen to the French so that I'm not going too fast. And if I do go too fast, I do hope an interpreter will let me know. Under 1, the HVO are apparently using Muslim males to dig trenches north of the Makljen Ridge. Were you aware of that happening?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: At the time I wasn't there, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. It's just before your period.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Just before my period. I think it's correct. We saw on both sides males digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Further down the page, under military activity, the HVO in Bugojno seemed to have withdrawn from some of their defence positions against BSA, apparently in order to tie down the BiH forces of Bugojno from reinforcing, i.e. Novi Travnik. Do you recollect anybody giving you that account of what the HVO had been doing?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of what they were exactly doing before I came in. My understanding is that they had some understanding what was -- of what was coming, and they were preparing, of course. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Towards the bottom we see something that we're going to see recurring perhaps later under other points, where we see that there was no possibility of seeing the imam of Prozor without the presence of HVO military police. Was that something that recurred as a problem, that you were kept away from the imam by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: When I was in Prozor in the beginning of my duty there, I went to the imam in Prozor several times, without problems; and after a period it was not allowed, and then it was allowed again, and so on and so on. So sometimes I could get in and sometimes not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I come to the next document, there's a general question I should ask you. In your time in the area, did the military authorities for the HVO to whom you spoke identify any politician to whom they referred?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, they spoke about Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: And such politicians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did they give any other name apart from Mate Boban of a local person or not or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, I think the last one we spoke about political matters, they talked about their own major in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, their own major?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was a military man?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Mayor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Can you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. I have it in the file somewhere, but I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't accept this if it isn't accurate, but for your purposes and during the time you were there, you dealt face to face with military men?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you personally and your fellow monitors didn't go behind the military men to see who was running things politically if anybody was?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. At the time I was in there, we didn't met political men, only on the level of the mayor and the priest and the imams and the military people there. We were more involved in the humanitarian and military matters than in political matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So if we go to the next document which is the 14th of July, the next page, under item 6, we see a report and this is still just before your time, a long time ago, Colonel Sileg had told UNPROFOR forces that HVO forces would give up Gornji Vakuf and move their main Defence back to Makljen Ridge in case Bugojno should fall to either the BSA or the BiH.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That didn't happen but they used Makljen Ridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you weren't aware, you or your fellow monitors, which, if any, politician would have been involved in that decision?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next page I think is the 15th of July and under one, "Bugojno is slightly tense due to a number of incidents which covers killings of three people, soldiers throwing civilians out of their apartments and small scale exchanges. The BSA shelling Bugojno started again with about 10 shells per day. Gornji Vakuf tense." And then under the political situation, "A so-called political meeting was held. The only political decision taken was that they continue with two parallel authority structures until a new political solution." So in your understanding, although the HVO were plainly outnumbered in due course, each side was still preparing.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Historically. So then we go over to the 16th of July -- it sets out unpredictability, I don't think I need trouble you with that. The next page is also the 16th of July. And makes it clear that "Bugojno," under number one, "is becoming more and more tense," and here is what I wanted to ask you about, this is under the authorship of your predecessor, but he does say there that there are Mujahedin soldiers in Bugojno and soldiers from the 7th Muslim Brigade. Now, do you know if that's a reflection of what he saw or if that's in any way his use of terminology or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I think it is his use of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Verhaag reminds me I should draw to your attention that what is underneath at the bottom of paragraph 3 when you go down about five lines it says, "UNPROFOR saw eight extremely well-armed Mujahedin soldiers in Bugojno today." So it may be that that makes it clear?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That is UNPROFOR soldier and he reports it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this was just before your time and you never saw them yourself?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I never saw them myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We also see under paragraph 3 this, "UNPROFOR have made the following observations of incoming troops in Prozor today." It sets out the soldiers and the guns and the trucks laden with ammunition. "They were well-dressed with new uniforms, new boots, no insignia. They are believed to be HV since they were drinking Tuborg beers which is brewed in Croatia and hard to get in Bosnia." Now, you remember His Honour Judge Robinson inquired whether there was materiel not to the level of proof that might have been available to you. Was it this sort of materiel that might have indicated the presence of HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: This kind of materiel is used in whole former Yugoslavia, and I think the beer is more interesting than the materiel, the military materiel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you think the beer might be significant?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite interesting for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Then we can go over to the 17th of July again, the same point that His Honour Judge Robinson raised, item 3, military activity, "An additional four to five busses full of soldiers have been seen west of Lake Ramsko moving towards Prozor." Would that be suggestive of HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, just a build up of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then on the 19th of July, there's an unauthored document, but I hope you will accept it for what it appears to be. Under 2, for the day it says this, a few lines down, middle of the page, "The BiH security officer in Travnik informed us that a Serb battalion with about 15 trucks have been seen to move on the area of Vlasic, Komar, Pogana and Ravan. He thinks that the Serbs won't attack against Bugojno with HVO groups." Would you be able to interpret that for us? It's just before you become active and start reporting. I wonder if you can help.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Give me some time. Well, I should interpret this in this way, now, at this time, maybe the BiH is searching for some reasons to start a defensive war and it is not a defensive war, could be, this is a possible interpretation because the BiH security officer told us so if it's true or not it's not confirmed, it's not a confirmed message and I think the BiH used this kind of information to have reason for starting the oncoming clashes, that is just possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it possible that there was --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: But you can also have another explanation, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that there was cooperation even at that stage between the Serbs and the HVO or the possibility of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The possibility of cooperation. We are not sure about that. The only proof we have that the Bosnian Serbs were helping the Croats was at the time the 12.000 people were fleeing, because they went from Bugojno, they went through Bosnian Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move to the next document which is the 19th of July, by the author Jacques Wirtgen, and we see under paragraph 1, a reference to still new confirmation of HV implication in Herzegovina. And then at the bottom of the page, we see this, more signs confirm -- perhaps I ought to read the whole of it, "According to Spanish battalion, the counter attack of HV or HVO south of Mostar in the region of Buna was rather successful. From the same source, it seems that the HVO Ljubina pocket would have been taken over by the Serb army. More signs confirm the collaboration HV HVO, for instance, an HV troop bus was observed today by M-3 when entering BH in the area of Neum 8 kilometres north of Ploca. Units from Zagreb would presently man the front line and then there's a number of vehicles with licence plates from Zagreb and Split." Now, I know this material wasn't handled by you directly, but that's rather more than just information, that's coming close to proof, isn't it, vehicles with plates with Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is coming more to proof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: But it is -- you can discuss about it of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Then on the next page, just for completeness, in the middle of the page back to the topic of Serb HVO cooperation, we see this, "But again it's according to the BiH security officer of Travnik, the Serb battalion would have been observed in the region west of Trube. He meant that this unit was going to Bugojno to join the HVO forces to attack the BiH." Then it says, "HVO launched a severe attack on the Muslim pocket in old Vitez." So as to the union of HVO and BSA, would your answer be the same as before that this might be the BiH officer setting up for a defensive action?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I didn't set up that it was to prepare for defensive action, only it is defensive actions are also an excuse for an offensive. That's what I meant. And maybe it's the same, maybe, because it wasn't at that time possible, to be possible for HVO troops. So if there were HV soldiers for both, it wasn't possible to go to Vitez at that time because they have to go through Muslim territory. I think for individuals it was possible, but not for great build up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look down the page we see the first, I think, account of the start of the Bugojno incident under the authorship of your colleague, where it says, "The most important event in the area," perhaps you see that, it's in the last big paragraph, "The most important event in the area was the start last night of a severe fighting in Bugojno. Those events seemed to have been the consequence of a single event at a checkpoint followed by escalation from both parties." Was that how the things seemed or was made to look as if it started?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: My opinion, it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: My opinion it is just an escalation, a clash at a checkpoint. I think it's not a correct interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you believe there was an intentional attack?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
